new_moe_models.analysis:
Qwen3-30B-A3B, released April 28–29 2025 by Alibaba, is the standout MoE model for local coding on Apple Silicon and AMD. It has 30.5B total parameters with only ~3.3B active per token (128 experts, 8 active), enabling dramatically reduced memory bandwidth requirements versus dense models. On 128GB unified memory systems, Q4_K_M quantization via MLX yields ~80–88 tok/s on M4 Max (546 GB/s bandwidth), ~70–76 tok/s on M3 Ultra, and ~68–70 tok/s on M2 Ultra. The model supports up to 131K token context windows comfortably on 128GB. HumanEval Pass@1 scores are competitive with GPT-4o class models among open-weight releases as of 2025, placing top 10–20 globally.

For AMD, the RX 7900 XTX (960 GB/s bandwidth, 24GB VRAM) achieves 65–90 tok/s for similarly sized Q4 GGUF models via ROCm/llama.cpp. The newer RDNA 4 RX 9070 XT (640 GB/s) sees 50–70 tok/s. Apple Silicon holds a stability and efficiency edge due to MLX's zero-copy unified memory architecture, while AMD requires careful ROCm setup. Both platforms handle 32K–128K context at Q4 with 128GB RAM.

Compared to a dense 30B model, Qwen3-30B-A3B's MoE design means ~60–70% fewer active FLOPs per token, translating to real-world throughput closer to a 7–10B dense model. The hybrid 'thinking/non-thinking' mode toggle adds further flexibility for coding vs. reasoning workloads. Q4_K_M is the recommended quantization for the best quality/speed balance; Q3_K_M saves ~15% more RAM at minor accuracy cost. On Apple Silicon, MLX backend consistently outperforms Ollama by 20–30% for this model class.

new_coding_models.analysis:
The leading new local coding models as of April 2026 are DeepSeek-R1 (671B full, but runnable at Q3/Q4 on 128GB for smaller distilled variants), Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct (detailed above), GLM-4.7 9B, and Kimi K2.5. GLM-4.7 9B (Zhipu AI) is a standout surprise: it achieves 94.2% HumanEval Pass@1 and 84.9 on LiveCodeBench, rivaling models 10x its size, and runs trivially on 128GB RAM under 16GB loaded. DeepSeek-R1 hits 92.0% HumanEval, with architecture estimated to be S-tier on SWE-bench Verified. Kimi K2.5 (Moonshot AI) leads SWE-bench Verified at 76.8% and LiveCodeBench at 85.0, but weights are not fully open-source for local use.

For 128GB RAM systems, the practical sweet spot is Qwen3-30B-A3B at Q4_K_M (~20GB loaded) for MoE efficiency, or DeepSeek-R1 distilled variants (7B–70B) which are available as GGUF via community releases. The full 671B DeepSeek-R1 requires aggressive Q2 quantization or multi-node to fit 128GB. OpenHands LM 32B is a new purpose-built SWE agent model on HuggingFace achieving 37%+ SWE-bench Verified resolve rate on open weights, ideal for agentic coding workflows. Q4_K_M or AWQ are the recommended quantization formats across all these models for the best quality/size tradeoff on Apple Silicon or AMD.

LiveCodeBench is now the discriminating benchmark as HumanEval has saturated (many models above 90%). For agentic/real-world tasks, SWE-bench Verified above 40% is considered production-grade for open models, with Kimi K2.5 at 76.8% representing the current ceiling. On 128GB RAM, users can run multiple smaller coding models simultaneously or a single large model with full 128K context via MLX or llama.cpp with GGUF.

mlx_llama_cpp.analysis:
MLX has emerged as the dominant inference runtime for Apple Silicon as of 2025–2026. Apple officially endorsed it at WWDC 2025 as the preferred on-device LLM runtime. Key advantages include true zero-copy unified memory (no PCIe bottleneck), lazy evaluation with kernel fusion, and dedicated Neural Accelerator support on M5 chips (2026). For models under 14B parameters, MLX outperforms llama.cpp by 20–87% in token generation throughput. Ollama switched to an MLX backend for Apple Silicon in 2025, yielding ~93% faster decode out of the box. Over 4,000 optimized MLX-quantized models are available on HuggingFace. Typical M4 Max speeds: 7B Q4 ~136 tok/s, 14B Q4 ~68 tok/s, 32B Q4 ~30 tok/s. A 2025 peer-reviewed study (arXiv:2511.05502) confirmed MLX achieves highest sustained throughput on Apple Silicon across model sizes tested on Mac Studio M2 Ultra.

llama.cpp (now under the ggml-org GitHub organization) continues rapid development into the b5000+ build range as of 2025. Key 2025 updates include: full GGUF format support with built-in HuggingFace model downloader, 1.5-bit and 2-bit experimental quantization options (alongside mature k-quants like Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M), Metal GPU offloading enabled by default on macOS (no manual flags needed), OpenAI-compatible llama-server REST API natively built-in, hybrid CPU+GPU partial offload for models larger than GPU memory, and Homebrew installation with automatic Metal support (`brew install llama.cpp`). New binary names: `llama-cli`, `llama-server`, `llama-bench`. For 32B+ models and long-context (>32K tokens) workloads, llama.cpp remains competitive with MLX due to mature GGUF quantization depth and flexible CPU offload.

The practical recommendation for 128GB Apple Silicon systems: use MLX (via mlx-lm pip package or Ollama) for models up to 30B for maximum speed; use llama.cpp for models requiring GGUF-specific quantizations (Q2_K, IQ3_XXS) to fit very large models (70B+) into available RAM. Both frameworks now support 100K+ token contexts with proper configuration.

coding_agents.analysis:
OpenHands 1.6.0 (released March 30, 2026) is the latest major version, adding support for Claude Opus 4.6, GLM-4.7, Kimi-K2.5, new `/clear` and `/new` workflow commands, hook support, and CVE patches. It fully supports YOLO/autonomous mode via local LLMs: recommended models are Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct, Devstral Small 2 (24B), and OpenHands LM 32B, served via LM Studio or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Docker-based deployment is fully documented. OpenHands LM 32B achieves 37%+ SWE-bench Verified resolve rate on open weights—competitive with much larger proprietary models—and is purpose-built for agentic coding tasks with 128K context.

SWE-agent has been superseded by mini-swe-agent (from Princeton NLP), which matches full SWE-agent performance with a simpler, more flexible architecture. It supports local and cloud LLMs natively and can run fully offline in YOLO/autonomous mode. Aider (latest versions in 2025–2026) added persistent code graphs for full-project context, native Llama 3 and Mistral support, and secure offline mode—making it the top choice for interactive CLI-based local coding assistance. Aider's 'architect mode' uses a strong model for planning and a faster local model for edits, which works well on 128GB systems.

GitHub Copilot Workspace has evolved significantly, offering 'PR-in-a-click' autonomous workflows similar to SWE-agent, with multi-step context-aware project changes, stronger refactoring, and test suite generation. It remains primarily cloud-based. The broader 2025–2026 trend is convergence: all major frameworks now support local LLMs, YOLO/autonomous modes, self-testing loops, and agentic multi-file editing. For fully private, local-only setups on 128GB Apple Silicon or AMD, the recommended stack is OpenHands 1.6 + LM Studio + Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct or OpenHands LM 32B.

recommendation.summary: The Mac Studio M4 Max 128GB is the best-fit device in your budget for 24/7 coding agents and 30B+ model inference, achieving ~87 tok/s on Qwen3-30B-A3B (MoE, 4-bit MLX). However, stock is severely constrained globally and in India, and the M5 Studio is expected at WWDC June 2026 or October 2026. AMD Strix Halo 128GB options far exceed your ₹3.5L ceiling in India.
recommendation.reasoning:
The Mac Studio M4 Max with 128GB unified memory is the only device currently within reach of your ₹1.5–3.5L budget that meets all your technical requirements. In the USA it lists at ~$3,499 (≈₹2.95L at current rates), which is inside budget if buying directly from the US Apple Store or a reseller like B&H Photo. India pricing for the M4 Max 128GB is not clearly published — Apple India's Mac Studio starts at ₹2,14,900 for base M4 Max (36GB) and M3 Ultra starts at ₹4,29,900. A custom 128GB M4 Max order via Apple India would likely land at ₹3.2–3.6L, pushing the top edge of your budget. The M3 Ultra starts above ₹4.29L — over budget. AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Strix Halo) 128GB laptops (ASUS ProArt, HP ZBook Ultra) are priced ₹6–8L in India — more than double your ceiling — and are scarce even at those prices, ruling them out entirely.

On the 'wait' angle: Mac Studio M5 Max/Ultra is widely expected at WWDC (June 8–12, 2026) or potentially delayed to October 2026 due to global LPDDR5X shortages per Mark Gurman. If announced in June, M5 Max will offer meaningfully higher memory bandwidth (~600+ GB/s vs M4 Max's 546 GB/s) and better neural engine throughput, likely pushing Qwen3-30B-A3B past 100 tok/s. It may also reset pricing, potentially making 128GB configs more accessible in India. If your need is truly urgent (production agents starting now), buy the M4 Max 128GB from the US. If you can wait 6–12 weeks, the M5 announcement will clarify whether to buy M4 Max at a possible discount or get the M5.

For fine-tuning: LoRA fine-tuning of 7B–30B models via MLX is very feasible on 128GB M4 Max. Full-parameter fine-tuning of 30B+ is impractical locally — use cloud (Lambda Labs, RunPod) for that. The 128GB gives comfortable headroom for LoRA on 30B models with batch size 1–2 and gradient checkpointing. MLX-LM's built-in LoRA trainer works out-of-the-box.

recommendation.fine_tuning: Highly feasible for LoRA/QLoRA on 7B–30B models using MLX-LM's built-in trainer. 128GB gives comfortable batch sizes and longer context during training. Full fine-tuning of 30B+ not practical locally — offload to cloud (RunPod A100 ~$1.5/hr). Recommended: mlx-lm fine_tune with lora_layers=16, batch_size=2, grad_checkpoint=True for Qwen3-30B-A3B.

Ollama 0.19 (Mar/Apr 2026) ships preview MLX backend for Apple Silicon — on M4 Max, decode speed nearly doubles from 58 to 112 tok/sec vs llama.cpp Metal backend; enable via env variable. MLX outperforms llama.cpp Metal by 20-87% on models under 14B params due to zero-copy unified memory. llama.cpp April 2026 updates focus on Metal runtime fixes, prefix caching fixes (critical for tool-calling/agents), and new GPU family + unified memory identification at llama-server startup. Recommended stack: Ollama+MLX backend for max throughput; llama.cpp for large models near RAM limits or cross-platform GGUF needs.
